units.title: The Sky
units.blurb: Read the turning sky, the seasons, the Moon's phases and eclipses from Earth's motions.

units.title: Gravity and Orbits
units.blurb: From Copernicus and Kepler to Newton: how planets move and how orbits weigh the heavens.

units.title: Light and Telescopes
units.blurb: Light is our messenger: its colors give temperatures, its lines give composition and its shifts give motion.

units.title: The Solar System
units.blurb: The planets, their moons and the small bodies, how they formed, and planets around other stars.

units.title: The Sun
units.blurb: Our star's layers, its fusion power, its lifetime and its magnetic activity.

units.title: Measuring the Stars
units.blurb: Distances, brightnesses, temperatures and masses of stars, and the H–R diagram that ties them together.

units.title: The Lives of Stars
units.blurb: How stars form, how long they last, and what they leave behind.

units.title: Galaxies and the Universe
units.blurb: Our galaxy, other galaxies, dark matter, and the expanding universe since the Big Bang.

topics.title: The Celestial Sphere
topics.short: The sky looks like a dome that turns once a day around the celestial poles, because Earth spins.
topics.trouble: Students think the stars themselves move across the sky each night, rather than Earth turning beneath them.

topics.title: Altitude, Azimuth and Your Latitude
topics.short: The North Star's altitude equals your latitude, and stars close enough to the pole never set.
topics.trouble: Students think the North Star is the brightest star, or that it sits overhead everywhere.

topics.title: Right Ascension and Declination
topics.short: Declination and right ascension are the sky's latitude and longitude, fixed to the stars.
topics.trouble: Students read right ascension hours as clock times of day.

topics.title: Solar and Sidereal Days
topics.short: Earth spins once in 23 h 56 min, but noon to noon takes 24 h because Earth also moves along its orbit.
topics.trouble: Students think one day is exactly one full spin of Earth.

topics.title: The Sun's Path Through the Year
topics.short: The Sun's declination swings between +23.4° and −23.4°, which sets the solstices, the equinoxes, the tropics and the polar circles.
topics.trouble: Students think the tropics and polar circles are arbitrary lines, rather than set by Earth's 23.4° tilt.

topics.title: The Sun's Noon Altitude
topics.short: The Sun's altitude at noon is 90° − latitude + the Sun's declination.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun passes straight overhead at noon everywhere, at least in summer.

topics.title: Moon Phases and Moonrise Times
topics.short: Each phase rises at its own time: a full Moon rises at sunset and a first-quarter Moon about noon, because of where the Moon sits relative to the Sun.
topics.trouble: Students think the Moon is only up at night, or that every phase rises at sunset.

topics.title: Synodic and Sidereal Months
topics.short: The phases repeat every 29.5 days, longer than the Moon's 27.3-day orbit, because Earth moves along its orbit too.
topics.trouble: Students think the cycle of phases takes exactly as long as one orbit of the Moon.

topics.title: Eclipse Seasons
topics.short: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°, so eclipses happen only near the two nodes, in eclipse seasons about six months apart.
topics.trouble: Students think there should be an eclipse every month, at every new and full Moon.

topics.title: From an Earth-Centered to a Sun-Centered Sky
topics.short: Retrograde loops and the phases of Venus favor Copernicus's Sun-centered model.
topics.trouble: Students think a planet really loops backward in space during retrograde motion, rather than Earth passing it.

topics.title: Kepler's First Law: Ellipses
topics.short: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, and eccentricity measures how stretched each one is.
topics.trouble: Students think planetary orbits are long, thin ellipses, when most are nearly circles.

topics.title: Kepler's Second Law: Equal Areas
topics.short: A planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest when nearest the Sun.
topics.trouble: Students think a planet moves at one steady speed around its orbit.

topics.title: Kepler's Third Law
topics.short: P² = a³ when the period is in years and the size of the orbit is in astronomical units.
topics.trouble: Students think a planet twice as far out takes twice as long, missing that it also moves more slowly.

topics.title: Weighing Stars and Planets with Orbits
topics.short: Newton's form of Kepler's third law, M = a³/P² in solar masses, AU and years, gives the mass at the center.
topics.trouble: Students think the orbiting body's own mass decides its period, when for a small satellite it hardly matters.

topics.title: Orbital Speed and Escape Speed
topics.short: A low circular orbit needs about 7.9 km/s at Earth, and escaping takes √2 times the circular speed.
topics.trouble: Students think a spacecraft must keep firing its engine to stay in orbit.

topics.title: Spring and Neap Tides
topics.short: When the Sun and Moon line up, their tides add to make spring tides; at the quarter Moons they partly cancel, making neap tides.
topics.trouble: Students think spring tides happen only in the spring.

topics.title: Looking Back in Time
topics.short: Light takes time to reach us (8.3 minutes from the Sun), so the farther we look, the older the view.
topics.trouble: Students think we see distant stars and galaxies as they are now, not as they were when the light left them.

topics.title: Color and Temperature: Wien's Law
topics.short: Hotter objects glow bluer: the peak wavelength is λ_peak = 2.9 × 10⁶ nm·K ÷ T.
topics.trouble: Students think red stars are the hottest because red looks "hot".

topics.title: Luminosity, Size and Temperature
topics.short: A star's power is L = 4πR²σT⁴, so in solar units L = R²T⁴.
topics.trouble: Students think a hotter star must always be more luminous, forgetting that size matters too.

topics.title: Spectral Lines and Kirchhoff's Laws
topics.short: Hot, dense objects give a continuous spectrum; thin gases give bright lines or, in front of a hotter source, dark lines.
topics.trouble: Students think dark lines mean the star lacks that element.

topics.title: The Doppler Shift of Light
topics.short: A spectral line's shift gives the speed toward or away from us: Δλ/λ = v/c.
topics.trouble: Students think a redshifted object looks red to the eye.

topics.title: Telescopes: Light-Gathering and Resolution
topics.short: A telescope's light-gathering power grows with the square of its diameter, and a bigger aperture shows finer detail.
topics.trouble: Students think a telescope's main job is to magnify.

topics.title: Observing Across the Spectrum
topics.short: Radio, infrared, X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes see what eyes can't, and some must fly above the air.
topics.trouble: Students think every telescope collects visible light, or that radio telescopes need to be in space.

topics.title: Planet Densities: Rock or Gas?
topics.short: A planet's mass and radius give its average density, about 4 to 5.5 g/cm³ for rocky planets and 0.7 to 1.6 g/cm³ for the giants.
topics.trouble: Students think the biggest planets must be the densest.

topics.title: How the Solar System Formed
topics.short: A spinning cloud flattened into a disk; rock and metal condensed near the Sun and ices farther out.
topics.trouble: Students think the planets formed from material thrown off the Sun.

topics.title: Comets and Meteor Showers
topics.short: Comets on long, stretched orbits grow tails that point away from the Sun, and Earth passing through their dust makes meteor showers.
topics.trouble: Students think a comet's tail streams out behind it along its path.

topics.title: Finding Planets Around Other Stars
topics.short: A passing planet dims its star by (R_planet/R_star)², and a planet's tug makes its star wobble.
topics.trouble: Students think most exoplanets were found by taking pictures of them.

topics.title: Layers of the Sun
topics.short: Energy made in the core moves out through the radiative and convective zones to the glowing photosphere.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun has a solid surface.

topics.title: How the Sun Shines
topics.short: Fusing hydrogen into helium turns about 0.7% of the mass into energy, by E = mc².
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun burns like a fire.

topics.title: The Sun's Lifetime
topics.short: Fuel divided by the rate of use gives the Sun about 10 billion years on the main sequence.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun will burn out within a few thousand years, or that it will explode as a supernova.

topics.title: Sunspots and the Solar Cycle
topics.short: Magnetic fields make cooler, darker sunspots, and solar activity rises and falls about every 11 years.
topics.trouble: Students think sunspots are hotter than the rest of the surface, or are holes in the Sun.

topics.title: Parallax and the Parsec
topics.short: A star's distance in parsecs is 1 divided by its parallax angle in arcseconds.
topics.trouble: Students think a larger parallax means a farther star.

topics.title: Brightness and Distance
topics.short: Apparent brightness falls off with the square of the distance: b = L/(4πd²).
topics.trouble: Students think a star twice as far away looks half as bright, instead of a quarter as bright.

topics.title: The Magnitude Scale
topics.short: Smaller magnitudes are brighter, and 5 magnitudes means 100 times the brightness.
topics.trouble: Students think a magnitude 6 star is brighter than a magnitude 1 star.

topics.title: Spectral Classes
topics.short: The classes O, B, A, F, G, K and M sort stars from hottest to coolest by their spectral lines.
topics.trouble: Students think the spectral classes are in alphabetical or size order.

topics.title: The H–R Diagram
topics.short: Plot luminosity against temperature to sort stars into the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.
topics.trouble: Students forget that temperature increases to the left on an H–R diagram.

topics.title: Binary Stars and Stellar Masses
topics.short: Two stars orbiting each other reveal their masses, and the main sequence turns out to be a sequence of mass.
topics.trouble: Students think stars on the main sequence differ only in age, not in mass.

topics.title: How Stars Are Born
topics.short: Gravity pulls cold clouds of gas and dust into protostars until their cores are hot enough for fusion.
topics.trouble: Students think stars form from the leftover pieces of planets.

topics.title: Main-Sequence Lifetimes
topics.short: A star's lifetime goes as its fuel over its luminosity, about M^(−2.5), so massive stars die young.
topics.trouble: Students think big stars last longer because they have more fuel.

topics.title: Red Giants and White Dwarfs
topics.short: When core hydrogen runs out a star swells into a red giant; a Sun-like star ends as an Earth-sized white dwarf.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun will end as a black hole or a supernova.

topics.title: Reading a Cluster's Age
topics.short: All stars in a cluster were born together, so the point where the main sequence ends gives its age.
topics.trouble: Students think a cluster's stars were born at different times, rather than together with different masses.

topics.title: Supernovae and the Elements
topics.short: Massive stars fuse elements up to iron, then their cores collapse and explode, spreading heavy elements into space.
topics.trouble: Students think a star can keep making energy by fusing iron.

topics.title: Neutron Stars and Pulsars
topics.short: A collapsed core can become a city-sized ball of neutrons spinning many times a second.
topics.trouble: Students think pulsars pulse because they swell and shrink, rather than sweep beams around like a lighthouse.

topics.title: Black Holes
topics.short: Within the event horizon, R = 2GM/c², not even light can escape, yet far away a black hole pulls like any other mass.
topics.trouble: Students think black holes are cosmic vacuum cleaners that pull in everything around them.

topics.title: The Milky Way
topics.short: Our galaxy is a disk of a few hundred billion stars, with the Sun about 26,000 light-years from the center.
topics.trouble: Students think the Milky Way is the whole universe, or that the Sun sits at its center.

topics.title: Kinds of Galaxies
topics.short: Spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies differ in shape, gas and the ages of their stars.
topics.trouble: Students think every galaxy is a spiral like ours.

topics.title: Dark Matter
topics.short: Stars and gas far out in galaxies orbit too fast for the mass we can see, so most of a galaxy's mass is dark.
topics.trouble: Students think dark matter is just ordinary dust and dim stars we haven't counted yet.

topics.title: Standard Candles
topics.short: Cepheid variables and type Ia supernovae have known luminosities, so how bright they look tells how far away they are.
topics.trouble: Students think every star of the same brightness in the sky is at the same distance.

topics.title: Hubble's Law
topics.short: Distant galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance: v = H₀d.
topics.trouble: Students think galaxies rush away from us because we sit at the center of the universe.

topics.title: The Age of the Universe
topics.short: Running the expansion backward, 1/H₀ gives an age of about 14 billion years.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the units of H₀, so their age comes out wrong by huge factors.

topics.title: Evidence for the Big Bang
topics.short: The expansion, the cosmic microwave background and the amounts of hydrogen and helium all point to a hot, dense early universe.
topics.trouble: Students picture the Big Bang as an explosion at one point in an empty space.

topics.title: The Accelerating Universe
topics.short: Distant supernovae show the expansion is speeding up, and we call the unknown cause dark energy.
topics.trouble: Students think the expansion must be slowing down because gravity pulls everything back.
